messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Pharmacist
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 58

He sits in the chair with his hands folded, thumbs rotating slowly around each other. The first thing he says is that he doesn’t know why he’s here—nothing happened to *him*. Then he stops, and for a long moment the only sound is the low hum of the air conditioner.

The event happened two years ago, on a Saturday afternoon in late summer. He was twenty-two, still living at home with his parents and his younger brother, Sione, who was sixteen. They’d gone to the beach together, something they’d done a hundred times before—a small cove on the south side of the island where the water was calm and shallow. He remembers the light, the way the sand sparkled. He’d been watching Sione body-surf, laughing at how the waves kept knocking him over. Then a single wave, bigger than the others, caught Sione off balance. He went under, and he didn’t come up.

He jumped in immediately. He could see Sione’s dark hair just below the surface, thrashing. He grabbed his brother’s arm, tried to pull him up, but Sione was panicked and stronger than he looked. They went under together. For a few seconds—maybe ten, maybe thirty—he couldn’t tell up from down. He remembers the salt burning his nose, the frantic kick of his brother’s legs against his stomach. Then a lifeguard pulled them both out. Sione was not breathing. He watched them pump his chest, watched his brother’s face turn from blue to gray. By the time the ambulance arrived, Sione was gone.

He has not been back to that beach, or any beach, since. The thought of it makes his stomach clench. He lives ten minutes from the coast now, but he takes the long way to work to avoid even the glimpse of the ocean through the buildings. If a friend mentions going sailing or snorkeling, he changes the subject quickly, or pretends he hasn’t heard. They don’t push. They know.

He works at a busy pharmacy in the mall. On the surface, he is good at his job—methodical, thorough, never makes a dosing error. But inside, he is always scanning. When a customer describes a medication that caused nausea or dizziness, a cold shock runs down his back. He double-checks every prescription three times, even the ones he could do in his sleep. His manager has noticed the extra time he takes, but she attributes it to conscientiousness. He doesn’t correct her.

At night, he dreams of water. He wakes gasping, sheets tangled around his legs, convinced he is drowning again. Sometimes the dream is him pulling Sione up from the surface and Sione is already dead, eyes open, mouth full of sand. Other times, it is Sione who saves him, and then he is the one dying, and the guilt is so sharp he cannot breathe. He tries to stay awake as long as possible—watching videos, playing games on his phone—but eventually sleep pulls him under.

His mother calls every Sunday. He lets it ring three extra times before picking up. She talks about the family, about church, about the garden. He answers in short sentences, asks polite questions, and when she says, “We miss you at the house” or “Are you eating properly?” he feels a tightness in his throat and says he has to go. He hasn’t cried since the funeral. He isn’t sure he can.

Last month, a woman he had been seeing for a few weeks asked if he wanted to go to the beach for the day. He said no, and when she pressed, he snapped at her, said something cruel. She left. He told himself it was for the best. He doesn’t deserve to be happy if Sione isn’t here. He could have done something differently—reached out with his other hand, not panicked, held him tighter. The logic doesn’t matter. The thought has become a room he lives in.

He is always tired. His shoulders are tight, his jaw aches from clenching. When a loud noise startles him in the pharmacy—a dropped bottle, a slammed drawer—he flinches hard enough that his elbow knocks a tray of pill vials off the counter. He apologizes, picks them up, and for the rest of the shift, his hands are not quite steady.

He is here because his older sister made the appointment. He doesn’t know what he expects—maybe a way to turn down the volume of his own mind, or permission to stop replaying that afternoon. He is not sure he can do either. But he came. That’s the only part of the story he has changed so far.
